column1: bash: what is IFS, and when does the shell use it?
column2:
IFS = Internal Field Separator — the chars bash splits an UNQUOTED expansion on.
Default: space, tab, newline.

Fires on unquoted  $var  $(cmd)  $@  $*  → chops them into words.
Quoting ("$var") turns splitting OFF.

Same IFS also JOINS: "${arr[*]}" / "$*" glue elements with IFS's first char.
(zsh does NOT auto-split unquoted expansions — this is bash behavior.)

column1: bash: the two IFS idioms — safe line read, and split a string on a delimiter
column2:
# 1) read a file line-by-line without mangling it:
while IFS= read -r line; do printf '%s\n' "$line"; done < file
     IFS=  (empty, this read only) -> don't trim leading/trailing whitespace
     -r                            -> backslash stays literal

# 2) split a string into an array on a delimiter:
csv="alpha,bravo,charlie"
IFS=, read -ra parts <<< "$csv"   # IFS=, this read only; -a array; <<< here-string
printf '%s\n' "${parts[@]}"      # alpha / bravo / charlie

Put IFS= on the SAME line as the command so it applies to just that command.
